# Merging Data {#sec-merging-data}

Data arrives in pieces: yields in one file, prices in another, weather in a third.  Answering
a real question usually means putting two or more of the pieces together.  This chapter
covers joins: how they work, how they fail, and how to check them.

## Learning Objectives {.unnumbered}

::: {.objectives}
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

1. Join two tables on a shared key with `left_join()` and friends.
2. Say what happens to rows that do not match, and check for them.
3. Explain why a join can return more rows than it started with.
4. Harmonize units and category names so that two real datasets can be merged.
:::

## Joining Two Tables {#sec-joins}

`XLOOKUP` (@sec-lookup) pulled a price across from a second table in Excel.  The R equivalent
is a **join**:

```r
library(tidyverse)

yields <- read_csv("data/field_yields.csv")
prices <- read_csv("data/crop_prices.csv")

yields |>
  left_join(prices, by = "crop")
```

The `by` argument names the **key**, the column both tables share, which decides which row
matches which.  Everything about joins comes back to the key.

### The four joins you need {.unnumbered}

They differ in which rows survive.

- **`left_join(a, b)`** keeps every row of `a` and fills in `NA` where `b` has no match. This
  is usually the one you want: your data stays intact and the extra columns come along.
- **`inner_join(a, b)`** keeps only rows that matched in both, and drops the rest without
  saying so.
- **`full_join(a, b)`** keeps everything from both, with `NA` wherever either side is missing.
- **`anti_join(a, b)`** keeps rows of `a` with no match in `b`. It returns no columns from `b`
  at all, which sounds useless until you need to find out what failed to match.

### Check what did not match {.unnumbered}

`left_join` does not complain when nothing matches.  It hands you a column of `NA` and lets you
carry on, so a join can fail completely without producing an error.

`anti_join` is how you look:

```r
yields |>
  anti_join(prices, by = "crop") |>
  distinct(crop)
```

Run that on real Saskatchewan data and the problem shows up straight away.  The variety trial
data calls it `"Canola/Rapeseed"` and the price list says `"Canola"`.  The trial says
`"Soybean"`, the prices say `"Soybeans"`.  Neither file is wrong.  They were written by
different people, and a join matches on exact text, so every canola row comes back with a
missing price.

Reconciling the categories is part of cleaning (@sec-cleaning, the next chapter).  Checking
before you assume the join worked is the habit worth building.

### The row-count trap {.unnumbered}

A join can return more rows than it started with.

This happens when the key is not unique in the second table.  If `prices` has one row per crop,
each yield row matches one price and the row count does not change.  If `prices` has one row
per crop *per year* and you join on crop alone, every yield row matches several price rows and
R returns all the combinations.  Sixty fields become two hundred and forty, and every summary
computed afterwards is wrong in a way that still looks plausible.

Check the count:

```r
nrow(yields)                                    # before
joined <- yields |> left_join(prices, by = "crop")
nrow(joined)                                    # after -- should be the same
```

If it grew, the key is incomplete.  Join on everything that identifies a row:

```r
yields |> left_join(prices, by = c("crop", "year"))
```

This is the composite key from @sec-lookup, where RM and year had to be glued together with `&`
to identify a row.  R lets you name several key columns instead of building one.

## A Worked Example: Canadian and US Canola Yields {#sec-canada-us-merge}

The Canadian and US canola data from @sec-getting-data make a realistic merge, because the
two tables agree on almost nothing: different column names, different units, different
geography labels.  The work before the join is most of the work.

Suppose the Canadian table has national average yield in kilograms per hectare, and the US
table reports pounds per acre.  Neither can be compared until both are in the same unit.
Prepare each table separately: keep the columns you need, convert to tonnes per hectare, and
give the yield column a name that says whose it is:

```r
canada <- canada_raw |>
  clean_names() |>
  filter(geo == "Canada") |>
  mutate(canada_t_ha = value / 1000) |>          # kg/ha -> t/ha
  select(year = ref_date, canada_t_ha)

us <- us_raw |>
  clean_names() |>
  mutate(us_t_ha = value * 0.00112) |>           # lb/ac -> t/ha
  select(year, us_t_ha)
```

Now the join is the easy part.  The key is `year`:

```r
both <- canada |>
  left_join(us, by = "year")

both
```

```
   year canada_t_ha us_t_ha
   <dbl>      <dbl>   <dbl>
 1  2015       1.85    1.66
 2  2016       2.06    1.71
 3  2017       2.28    1.87
 ...
```

One table, one row per year, both countries' yields in the same unit.  Run the checks anyway:
`nrow(both)` should equal `nrow(canada)`, and `anti_join(canada, us, by = "year")` shows any
years one source has and the other does not -- a data release usually lags a year on one side
or the other, and it is better to find that now than in a chart.
